cards: Philip II was King of Spain from 1556 to 1598, ruling the Spanish Empire at the height of its power.
Akbar was the third Mughal emperor, reigning from 1556 to 1605.
Martin Luther was a German theologian and monk whose Ninety-five Theses of 1517 began the Protestant Reformation.
Hernán Cortés was a Spanish conquistador who led the expedition that brought down the Aztec Empire between 1519 and 1521.
Babur was a Timurid prince from Central Asia, descended from Timur and Genghis Khan, who founded the Mughal Empire.
Francis I, Duke of Nevers, born François de Clèves, was a French nobleman and soldier of the house of Cleves, which had held the county of Nevers since 1491.
Bayinnaung was king of the First Toungoo Empire of Burma from 1550 to 1581, and created what may have been the largest empire in the history of South-East Asia.
Vasco da Gama was a Portuguese navigator who led the first European voyage to reach India by sea, arriving at Calicut in 1498 after rounding the Cape of Good Hope.
Henry IV of France was king of Navarre from 1572 and the first Bourbon king of France from 1589.
Elizabeth I was Queen of England and Ireland from 1558 to 1603, the last Tudor monarch.
Desiderius Erasmus of Rotterdam was a Dutch humanist scholar, the most famous of the Northern Renaissance.
Niccolò Machiavelli was a Florentine diplomat, historian and political theorist.
Túpac Amaru was the last Sapa Inca of the Neo-Inca State of Vilcabamba, ruling from 1571 to 1572.
Ismail I was the founder of the Safavid dynasty, who took Tabriz and was proclaimed shah in 1501.
Atahualpa was the last Sapa Inca of the Inca Empire before the Spanish conquest.
Henry VIII of England reigned from 1509.
Miguel de Cervantes was a Spanish novelist, playwright and poet, the greatest writer of the Spanish Golden Age.
John III was King of Portugal from 1521 to 1557.
Gustav I, known as Gustav Vasa, was a Swedish nobleman who led the revolt against Christian II after the Stockholm Bloodbath of 1520 and was elected king of Sweden in 1523, ending the Kalmar Union.
John Calvin was a French theologian and reformer whose Institutes of the Christian Religion became a founding text of Reformed Protestantism.
Ahmad ibn Ibrahim al-Ghazi, known as Ahmad Gragn, was the imam and military leader of the Adal Sultanate who led a jihad against the Ethiopian Empire from 1527 to 1543.
Huáscar was Sapa Inca of the Inca Empire from about 1527 to 1532, ruling from Cuzco after the death of his father Huayna Capac.
John Zápolya was Voivode of Transylvania from 1510 and, after the death of Louis II at Mohács in 1526, was elected King of Hungary by the nobles as John I.
Pedro Álvares Cabral was a Portuguese navigator who reached the coast of Brazil in 1500 while leading a fleet to India.
Afonso I of Kongo, also known as Nzinga Mbemba, was king of the Kongo Empire from 1509 to 1543.
Henry II of France, son of Francis I, was king of France from 1547 to 1559.
Michelangelo Buonarroti (1475–1564) was a Florentine sculptor, painter, architect and poet, one of the greatest artists of the Italian Renaissance.
Nuño Beltrán de Guzmán was a Spanish conquistador and colonial official in Mexico.
Raphael (Raffaello Sanzio) was an Italian painter and architect of the High Renaissance, born in Urbino in 1483.
Sigismund II Augustus was King of Poland and Grand Duke of Lithuania, the last of the Jagiellonian dynasty, who died in 1572.
Diego de Landa was a Spanish Franciscan friar and later Bishop of Yucatán.
Felipe Guaman Poma de Ayala was an Andean nobleman of Peru who wrote the Nueva corónica y buen gobierno, a chronicle of about 1,200 pages addressed to the king of Spain around 1615.
Huayna Capac was the Sapa Inca who ruled the Inca Empire at its greatest extent, from about 1493.
Johannes Bugenhagen was a Pomeranian theologian, close colleague of Martin Luther and pastor of Wittenberg, known as Doctor Pomeranus.
John of Austria was an illegitimate son of the Emperor Charles V, recognised by his half-brother Philip II of Spain.
Pedro de Alvarado was a Spanish conquistador and lieutenant of Hernán Cortés in the conquest of the Aztec Empire, after which he subdued Tututepec.
Tycho Brahe was a Danish nobleman and astronomer.
Albert, Duke of Prussia, a Hohenzollern of the Ansbach line, was the last Grand Master of the Teutonic Order in Prussia.
Diego de Almagro was a Spanish conquistador and partner of Francisco Pizarro in the conquest of Peru.
Francis Xavier was a Navarrese priest and co-founder of the Society of Jesus who became the leading Catholic missionary in Asia.
